title: Fencing: overview
d: Fencing is a combat sport played 1 per side.
definition: Fencing is a combat sport played 1 per side.
description: Fencing is a combat sport. score more touches than the opponent. The contest is played 1 per side, and the side that first to 15 touches (or most in time); team bouts to 45 wins. Modern sport from 19th-century dueling schools; Olympic since the first 1896 Games. The sport is governed by official laws that cover the field of play, equipment, players, officials, scoring, fouls, and conduct; this database walks through every one of those areas so a newcomer can follow a full match with understanding.

title: The objective
d: The objective of Fencing is: score more touches than the opponent.
definition: The objective of Fencing is: score more touches than the opponent.
description: Every rule in Fencing exists to serve one objective: score more touches than the opponent. All tactics, positions, and scoring flow from that single aim. Beginners should fix the objective in mind first, because every foul, stoppage, and strategy in the sport is judged against whether it fairly advances or unfairly blocks that objective. Coaches return to it constantly: if a play does not serve the objective, it is the wrong play.

facts.objective: score more touches than the opponent

title: Scoring system
d: In Fencing, scoring works as follows: first to 15 touches (or most in time); team bouts to 45.
definition: In Fencing, scoring works as follows: first to 15 touches (or most in time); team bouts to 45.
description: Scoring in Fencing: first to 15 touches (or most in time); team bouts to 45. Knowing exactly what counts, and how much, changes how you watch: every attack is shaped by the scoring system, and comebacks are measured against it. Scorekeepers record each score the moment it happens, and at most levels the scoreboard is the official record unless a protest is filed under the competition rules.

facts.scoring: first to 15 touches (or most in time); team bouts to 45

title: How games are won
d: Fencing: first to 15 touches (or most in time); team bouts to 45.
definition: Fencing: first to 15 touches (or most in time); team bouts to 45.
description: Winning Fencing comes down to the scoreboard: first to 15 touches (or most in time); team bouts to 45. Because of that, late-game strategy everywhere in the sport is clock-and-score management — protecting a lead or chasing one changes every decision, from how much risk to take to when to slow play down or speed it up. Champions are often simply the teams that manage the winning condition best in the final minutes.

title: Ties and tiebreakers
d: Tied games in Fencing are resolved under the competition rules for the level of play.
definition: Tied games in Fencing are resolved under the competition rules for the level of play.
description: Not every contest in Fencing can end tied: league games may allow draws while knockout games must produce a winner through extra time, tiebreak procedures, or shootouts defined by the competition. Tiebreak rules are announced before play and never invented mid-game; players and coaches must know them, because they reshape tactics — a team may play for penalties, or gamble everything to avoid them.

facts.note: tiebreak rules are set by the competition, not improvised

title: Match duration
d: Fencing contests last: 3 periods of 3 minutes.
definition: Fencing contests last: 3 periods of 3 minutes.
description: A Fencing contest runs 3 periods of 3 minutes. Duration shapes fitness demands: athletes train to be sharp in the final stretch, not just the first. Timekeeping is an official duty — the clock, not the players, decides when it ends, and added or extra time exists to compensate for stoppages so the advertised duration is genuinely played.

title: Periods and breaks
d: Play in Fencing is divided into periods with breaks as defined for the competition.
definition: Play in Fencing is divided into periods with breaks as defined for the competition.
description: The 3 periods of 3 minutes in Fencing give coaches their main lever: adjustments, substitutions, and rest happen in the breaks. Teams plan for three phases — start fast, manage the middle, finish strong — and the side that uses its breaks better often wins the second half. Break length and number are fixed by the rules; exceeding them can draw penalties.

title: The venue
d: Fencing is played at: piste 14m long, 1.5-2m wide.
definition: Fencing is played at: piste 14m long, 1.5-2m wide.
description: The Fencing is part of the sport: piste 14m long, 1.5-2m wide. Dimensions, surfaces, and markings are standardized so records and tactics transfer between venues. Groundskeepers and officials inspect the venue before play; an unfit surface can postpone a contest. Players learn to read their venue — wind, sun, surface speed — because the same game plays differently in different buildings.

title: Field dimensions
d: Regulation dimensions for Fencing: piste 14m long, 1.5-2m wide.
definition: Regulation dimensions for Fencing: piste 14m long, 1.5-2m wide.
description: Regulation Fencing dimensions: piste 14m long, 1.5-2m wide. Lines are part of the field of play and officiated precisely — in or out, over the line or not, decides scores. Youth and amateur versions scale the dimensions down, but the proportions and the meaning of every line stay the same so skills transfer up to the full-size game.

title: Playing surface
d: Fencing surfaces must be safe, level, and marked to regulation.
definition: Fencing surfaces must be safe, level, and marked to regulation.
description: The playing surface in Fencing must be safe, level, and marked to regulation. Surface changes tactics: fast surfaces reward speed and quick passing, slow or soft ones reward power and patience. Footwear and equipment rules usually assume a specific surface, and playing on the wrong one risks both injury and disqualification of the contest.

title: Essential equipment
d: Fencing requires: mask, jacket, glove, weapon (foil, epee, sabre), electronic scoring.
definition: Fencing requires: mask, jacket, glove, weapon (foil, epee, sabre), electronic scoring.
description: No one plays Fencing without: mask, jacket, glove, weapon (foil, epee, sabre), electronic scoring. Equipment is inspected — illegal or unsafe gear is removed before play, and at higher levels every item must meet the governing body's specifications. Beginners should buy for safety and fit first, performance second; the right size matters more than the brand.

facts.equipment: mask, jacket, glove, weapon (foil, epee, sabre), electronic scoring

title: The ball
d: The Fencing ball is specified by the laws: size, weight, and pressure are regulated.
definition: The Fencing ball is specified by the laws: size, weight, and pressure are regulated.
description: Where Fencing uses a ball, its size, weight, bounce, and pressure are fixed by the laws: mask, jacket, glove, weapon (foil, epee, sabre), electronic scoring. Ball specs change the whole game — a lighter, livelier ball rewards touch, a heavier one rewards power. Match balls are approved and often supplied by the competition; warming up with the wrong spec builds the wrong feel.

facts.equipment: mask, jacket, glove, weapon (foil, epee, sabre), electronic scoring

title: Protective gear
d: Protection in Fencing: required and recommended gear keeps players safe within the laws.
definition: Protection in Fencing: required and recommended gear keeps players safe within the laws.
description: Protection is part of the laws of Fencing, not an afterthought. Required and recommended gear exists because the sport's known injury patterns are known: the rules mandate the gear that prevents the common ones. Gear must fit and be worn correctly — loose or missing protection can keep a player off the field, and no contest is worth a preventable injury.

title: Team size
d: Fencing is played 1 per side.
definition: Fencing is played 1 per side.
description: Fencing is played 1 per side. Numbers decide the geometry of the game: more players means more structure and specialization, fewer means more space and versatility. Every player must know the legal team size, because playing short — or with too many — brings penalties, and planned rotations are built around the allowed numbers.

title: Positions and roles
d: Positions in Fencing divide the work: each role has a zone, duties, and skills.
definition: Positions in Fencing divide the work: each role has a zone, duties, and skills.
description: Positions in Fencing exist to divide the 1 per side into manageable jobs. Each role has a home zone, primary duties, and a skill profile; great teams are built by fitting people to roles, not roles to people. Beginners should learn one position deeply before roaming — mastery of a role teaches the whole game faster than playing everywhere badly.

title: Substitutions
d: Substitution rules in Fencing control how and when players may be replaced.
definition: Substitution rules in Fencing control how and when players may be replaced.
description: Substitutions in Fencing are a tactical weapon governed by strict procedure: only at stoppages, only through the official, only within the allowed number. Coaches plan substitution windows the way generals plan reserves — fresh legs at the right moment win tight games. Illegal substitution procedure can cost a team a player or a penalty.

title: Officials
d: Fencing is officiated by: referee plus scoring apparatus.
definition: Fencing is officiated by: referee plus scoring apparatus.
description: Fencing is officiated by referee plus scoring apparatus. Officials are neutral arbiters of the laws: their decisions on matters of fact are final during play, and dissent is penalized. Knowing what each official watches helps players stay legal — most fouls are committed in full view of exactly the official assigned to that zone.

title: The referee's role
d: The referee in Fencing enforces the laws, keeps time, and manages conduct.
definition: The referee in Fencing enforces the laws, keeps time, and manages conduct.
description: The referee's job in Fencing is bigger than blowing a whistle: enforcing the laws, keeping time, managing conduct, and protecting player safety — in that order. Players may ask for clarification respectfully; they may not dispute decisions. At every level, the referee's authority begins when they enter the venue and ends when they leave it.

title: Key rule 1
d: Foil: torso only, right-of-way rules decide simultaneous hits.
definition: Foil: torso only, right-of-way rules decide simultaneous hits.
description: Key rule of Fencing (1 of 4): Foil: torso only, right-of-way rules decide simultaneous hits.. This is one of the laws players break most often when learning the game, so officials watch it closely. Understanding the reason behind the rule — the unfair advantage it prevents — makes it easy to remember and to apply at speed. When in doubt during play, the safe choice is the one this rule describes.

facts.rule: Foil: torso only, right-of-way rules decide simultaneous hits.

title: Fouls
d: Illegal play in Fencing draws fouls under the laws; persistent fouling draws cards or ejections.
definition: Illegal play in Fencing draws fouls under the laws; persistent fouling draws cards or ejections.
description: A foul in Fencing is illegal play as defined by the laws — not just rough play, but any act the rules forbid. Officials grade fouls by intent, danger, and advantage gained; persistent or cynical fouling draws escalating punishment. Smart players learn the exact line: physical right up to it, never across it.

title: Penalties
d: Fouls in Fencing are punished by free plays, spot penalties, or loss of possession per the laws.
definition: Fouls in Fencing are punished by free plays, spot penalties, or loss of possession per the laws.
description: Punishment in Fencing fits the foul: minor infringements restart play for the other side, serious ones award direct scoring chances or remove the offender. Penalty rules are deliberately severe enough that fouling is never a good trade — the team that stays disciplined keeps eleven (or its equivalent) on the field and wins the close ones.

title: Discipline and conduct
d: Misconduct in Fencing — dissent, dangerous play, unsporting behavior — is penalized, up to ejection.
definition: Misconduct in Fencing — dissent, dangerous play, unsporting behavior — is penalized, up to ejection.
description: The laws of Fencing punish misconduct on a ladder: warnings, cards, sin-bins, ejections, suspensions. Dissent, dangerous play, and unsporting behavior are treated as seriously as technical fouls, because the game depends on respect for officials and opponents. Captains are responsible for their team's conduct and speak to the referee for the side.

title: Basic strategy
d: Fencing strategy starts from the objective: score more touches than the opponent.
definition: Fencing strategy starts from the objective: score more touches than the opponent.
description: All Fencing strategy serves the objective: score more touches than the opponent. The basic game plan is simple — win your individual battles, keep your shape, and take the chances the scoring system rewards most. Beginners win by doing simple things reliably; advanced players win by forcing opponents into mistakes while making none themselves.

facts.objective: score more touches than the opponent

title: Offense
d: Attacking in Fencing means creating the scoring chances the rules reward.
definition: Attacking in Fencing means creating the scoring chances the rules reward.
description: Attacking Fencing is about manufacturing the highest-percentage chances the scoring system allows. Good offense is patient until the opening appears, then ruthless: create space, move the defense, and finish. The best attacks look simple because every player knows the plan two passes ahead.

title: Defense
d: Defending in Fencing means denying the objective: score more touches than the opponent.
definition: Defending in Fencing means denying the objective: score more touches than the opponent.
description: Defending Fencing starts from denying the objective: score more touches than the opponent. Good defense is organized first and aggressive second — shape, communication, and patience, with pressure applied where the opponent is weakest. The great defensive teams all share one trait: every player defends, all the time, without being asked.

facts.objective: score more touches than the opponent

title: Origins
d: Origins of Fencing: Modern sport from 19th-century dueling schools; Olympic since the first 1896 Games..
definition: Origins of Fencing: Modern sport from 19th-century dueling schools; Olympic since the first 1896 Games..
description: The origins of Fencing: Modern sport from 19th-century dueling schools; Olympic since the first 1896 Games.. Like most sports, it began as folk play and was formalized when clubs and schools wrote common rules so strangers could compete fairly. Those first written laws are the ancestor of every rule in this database — the game you watch today is their descendant.

facts.history: Modern sport from 19th-century dueling schools; Olympic since the first 1896 Games.

title: Modern era
d: Modern Fencing: professional leagues, world championships, and Olympic or global stages.
definition: Modern Fencing: professional leagues, world championships, and Olympic or global stages.
description: Modern Fencing grew through professional leagues, world championships, and global competition. Television and professionalism standardized the laws worldwide and turned the best players into full-time athletes. The modern game is faster, stronger, and more tactical than any earlier era — but it is played under the same essential objective the founders wrote down.

title: Variations
d: Fencing has official and informal variations with adjusted rules for numbers, space, and level.
definition: Fencing has official and informal variations with adjusted rules for numbers, space, and level.
description: Every major sport spawns variations: small-sided, beach, indoor, youth, and disability versions of Fencing all adjust numbers, space, and rules while keeping the soul of the game. Variations are where most people actually play — the full eleven-a-side (or equivalent) version is the tip of a much bigger pyramid.

title: Safety
d: Play Fencing safely: warm up, wear the required gear, follow the foul laws, and stop for injury.
definition: Play Fencing safely: warm up, wear the required gear, follow the foul laws, and stop for injury.
description: Safety in Fencing is part of the rules, not separate from them: warm up properly, wear every required piece of gear, respect the foul laws that exist to prevent injury, and stop play for any head injury or suspected serious harm. No game, drill, or tryout is worth playing hurt — the laws protect players who protect themselves.
